identity: A single classical hadith (Sahih al-Bukhari, Kitab al-Iman: the report of Talha b. Ubaydallah about the dishevelled man of Najd who came questioning the Prophet about Islam). Classical Arabic hadith prose in the standard two-part shape: an isnad / transmission chain (Ismail > Malik b. Anas > his uncle Abu Suhayl b. Malik > his father > Talha b. Ubaydallah) running without break into the matn, whose body is almost entirely reported dialogue framed by qala / faqala. One paragraph, no <NL> tokens, 130 tokens indexed 0-129. Register: 3rd-century-AH compilation Arabic, oral-report style, paratactic, with no subordinating apparatus beyond hatta, fa-idha and hal clauses.
law: The sentence unit of this text is the SPEECH TURN or the completed narrative predication. Concretely: (1) the isnad is never cut - its links (qala, an, annahu samia) are comma-level joints, and a verbum dicendi that still owes its reported complement (yaqul at 21, yaqul at 112) can never end a sentence, so the chain flows unbroken into the opening of the matn; (2) inside the narrative setup, nat/hal material (thair al-ras, yasmau dawiyya sawtihi wa-la yufqahu ma yaqul), hatta-clauses and fa-idha continuations are all sentence-internal; (3) every change of speaker closes a sentence - the turn ends on the last word of the reported speech, and the next qala/faqala that introduces the new turn opens the next sentence; (4) a hal-headed interrogative is a complete illocutionary act and closes its sentence even when the reply follows immediately in a bare qala; (5) a narrating qala (Talha reporting: qala wa-dhakara lahu..., qala fa-adbara al-rajul...) does not itself take a boundary - the break falls before it, not on it; (6) internal coordination (wa-la yufqahu, wa-la anqusu), exception phrases (illa an tattawwaa) and conditional tails (in sadaqa) never break.
reasoning: Hard sites argued. (a) Index 21 yaqul: tempting as the isnad/matn seam, but yaqul governs the following reported clause (jaa rajul...) and cannot stand without it; the seam is a colon, not a stop. No boundary - high confidence. (b) Indices 33/35/38/42/44 inside jaa rajul...an al-islam: min ahl najd and thair al-ras are stacked descriptions of rajul; yasmau dawiyya sawtihi wa-la yufqahu ma yaqul is a circumstantial hal clause; hatta dana is subordinate; fa-idha huwa yasal is the fa-of-surprise completing it. The whole arrival scene is one long sentence, 0-49, closing on al-islam at 49 immediately before the full attribution faqala rasul Allah - a very clean break. (c) The decisive recurring site, indices 65 / 83 / 102 (ghayruha / ghayruhu). This single decision carries three of twelve boundaries. Two readings compete. Reading A (speech-turn): hal is an unambiguous interrogative particle, the mans question is a closed independent act, and the bare qala that follows is a change of speaker introducing the reply - speaker change plus closed interrogative is the strongest boundary evidence dialogue prose offers, and any punctuation scheme that survives stripping would have put a question mark there. Reading B (exchange unit): the older hadith-typesetting habit lets the full stop fall only after the closing quotation mark of the Prophets words, so that question and answer share one stop and the unit runs faqala hal alayya ghayruha qala la illa an tattawwaa. I take Reading A: the interrogative is too strongly marked to leave unstopped, and Reading B is an artifact of a quotation convention rather than of sentence structure. Marked med, because a source edition following Reading B is the one thing that would flip these three. (d) Index 98 al-zakat: qala wa-dhakara lahu rasul Allah ... al-zakat is narration, not quoted speech, and closes a complete predication; the next qala opens the mans turn. Boundary, med - it is secure under Reading A and merely likely under Reading B. (e) Indices 89 and 108: these qala tokens are Talhas narrating verb, complement-bearing, so no boundary sits on them; the break falls at 88 and 107 respectively, on tattawwaa, just before them. (f) Index 67 la: qala la illa an tattawwaa is one utterance - the exception phrase completes the negation, so no break after la. (g) Indices 110/112/117: fa-adbara al-rajul wa-huwa yaqul is a hal construction, yaqul again owes its complement (wallahi la azidu...), and la azidu ala hadha wa-la anqusu is one coordinated oath. The turn runs 108-119 whole, closing on anqusu. (h) Index 127 aflaha: in sadaqa is its conditional tail, sentence-internal; 129 sadaqa is the mandatory final boundary.
